passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Pradeep (Class 11) came in with a sheet listing his coaching batches in two columns: “explains new ideas” and “repeats what school already did”. The physics problem-solving batch and the chemistry doubts class went in the first column; the maths revision batch went in the second. He said he had been awake past one every night. I asked what he wanted to do. He chose to keep the first two and drop maths revision, then planned to use the freed evenings for solving his own problems and going to bed earlier. I asked how he would know it worked; he suggested comparing test scores after a month. I have asked his parents to come in on the 14th so we can review it together. — Rafiq

Wednesday night

I finally did it. I dropped the chemistry batch at the coaching centre and the maths crash course.

Mahima di said last week: "Which ones actually teach you something new?" So for three days I marked every class. Physics batch: clears concepts I never got in school. Keep. Biology batch: great practice questions. Keep. Chemistry batch: honestly, it repeats Mrs. Iyer's lectures word for word. Maths crash course: the same problems as our school worksheet.

Tonight I told Amma and she agreed, as long as I use the time properly.

So now: two batches instead of four. That's five free hours. Two go to self-study, working through my own doubts, one hour every evening. The rest goes to sleep. Real sleep, before eleven.

I'm Usha, and I feel slightly guilty, like I'm cheating. But I also feel like I can breathe.

qa.q: How many free hours did Usha gain?
How does Usha feel about dropping the two classes?
qa.a: Usha feels slightly guilty, as if cheating, but also relieved enough to breathe.

qa.q: What else could Usha do to check the choice was right?
qa.a: Usha could compare test scores and energy after a month, and discuss the result with Amma and Mahima di.

qa.q: How might Mahima di see Usha's decision?
qa.a: Mahima di would probably feel pleased, since her question about new learning led to a clear, reasoned choice.

grounding: A diary shows a student comparing which coaching batches clarify concepts and which repeat school content, keeping the most useful and using freed time for self-study and sleep.
